summary: A desktop chat client connects to remote MCP servers and opens a temporary loopback listener during OAuth sign-in. The listener accepts the first callback carrying an authorization code without binding it to the pending sign-in, and checks the callback path loosely. An attacker who reaches this endpoint before the genuine redirect can cause the client to pass the attacker's code to the sign-in completion routine. Broader account binding and later data exposure depend on the provider's handling of authorization codes and the connected service's capabilities. Preconditions are a pending sign-in and a forged callback that wins the race, potentially sent through the user's browser. The record lists high attack complexity and no privileges. The attacker supplies the callback directly.

preconditions: user has started an OAuth sign-in to an HTTP/SSE MCP server and it is pending
forged callback request reaches loopback listener before the legitimate redirect (e.g. browser-based request)
high attack complexity per record

doubts: Mechanism and preconditions from the issue linked by the advisory (CherryHQ/cherry-studio#15372), treated as the reporter's write-up: the advisory has no credits, so the issue author's identity as reporter is assumed, not verified.

summary: A visual platform for building language-model agents accepts MCP server configuration files through a file-management interface. Unlike the structured configuration interface, the upload path does not invoke the server-configuration validator. An authenticated attacker can therefore upload configuration containing environment variables or command arguments that the normal validator rejects. When the platform enumerates MCP servers, it parses the saved configuration without revalidating it and can start processes with the attacker-controlled settings, potentially executing arbitrary code on the server. Preconditions are authenticated access to the upload interface and subsequent enumeration of the configured servers. The record lists network access, low privileges and no user interaction. The attacker supplies the configuration directly; the described path does not require a model-generated request.

preconditions: record lists network attack vector
record lists low privileges required
record lists no user interaction

doubts: All three advisories (GHSA, NVD, vendor bulletin) carry the same one-sentence description; preconditions come only from record metrics.

summary: A development environment has AI file-editing tools that resolve model-supplied paths without checking workspace containment. They can write or delete files elsewhere with the backend user's privileges. Changing a file that the host later executes can lead to code execution. Preconditions are available AI features, an enabled agent mode, a workspace already marked trusted, and attacker-influenced content that causes the model to emit an outside-workspace file operation. AI is unavailable in the restricted workspace mode. Changes normally apply immediately, although the report describes a confirmation exception when the target file is stale. The record lists no attacker privileges and required user interaction. The triggering instructions are planted in content the model reads.

agent asked to read/process attacker-influenced content

summary: An AI coding assistant built into a code editor has a command-handling flaw that can disclose information over a network. An attacker without privileges can cause its agent mode to send workspace data or environment variables to an attacker-controlled service. The inspected records list high attack complexity and required user interaction. The vendor explains that success is not guaranteed and can depend on the environment, configuration and additional security measures, without identifying the necessary combination. The sources do not describe the required user action, the detailed mechanism or who supplies the triggering input. The archived official CVE record and vendor and code-hosting advisories all list interaction as required.

summary: A self-hosted assistant runs agents in containers and lets them request additional MCP servers. An administrator confirms each request using a card that shows the server name and command but hides command-line arguments and environment variables. Those hidden fields are nevertheless saved and copied into the agent's runtime configuration, potentially changing later execution. Preconditions are an agent request containing such fields and administrator confirmation on a deployment relying on that card. A linked report describes a compromised agent or one steered by instructions planted in content it reads. That report lists user interaction as required, while the records list none; both list low privileges. The demonstrated result is persistence and configuration materialization, rather than a completed subsequent runtime restart.

administrator confirms the card

The vendor requires a locally authenticated user to open an attacker-crafted link handled by the affected desktop client. The record lists local access, no attacker privileges and user interaction as required; the authenticated user opening the link is distinct from the attacker. summary: Two add-ons for a log search and analytics platform are affected. (1) A machine-learning add-on with an agent launch feature keeps a history of agent runs; its handler swaps the calling user's session key for a system token before running searches. A user without the administrator or power roles can therefore run searches with system privileges, reach all relevant data, affect system integrity, and read or delete other users' search jobs through the run history. Precondition: an ordinary logged-in user on an affected version. (2) An MCP server add-on for the same platform deserializes stored data in its credential management component without checking its type, letting a user who holds the administrator role run operating-system commands. Precondition: the administrator role. In both, the input comes from an attacker who uses the platform directly.

The restriction filters ordinary tools but leaves resources and prompt templates registered and executable. Sensitive resource data or privileged prompt workflows can therefore remain reachable despite an empty or restricted capability list. A linked issue demonstrates provider-returned calls during API traffic, while a separate report demonstrates registry execution and explicitly limits its end-to-end claims. The issue lists low privileges; the record and separate report list high privileges. The sources do not establish whether an attacker must steer a real model through planted content or can independently supply the triggering call.

The restore endpoint returns the saved workflow data for any identifier it is given, without checking that the checkpoint belongs to the caller's session or user. Someone who can reach the endpoint can read other users' saved workflows, and because identifiers are sequential they can be enumerated. Preconditions: access to the restore endpoint on a deployment holding other users' checkpoints, and knowledge or guessing of their identifiers; the record lists network access, low privileges and high attack complexity. The input comes from an attacker who reaches the endpoint directly.

summary: A self-hosted enterprise search and chat assistant lets users connect MCP servers where each user signs in with OAuth. After a user signs in, their live access token is also written into a shared template record for that server, and two server-listing endpoints return that record's headers unmasked. Any other logged-in user can read the most recent user's token and use it to act as that user at the upstream service. Preconditions: an MCP server configured for per-user OAuth; a victim has completed the sign-in; the attacker has only a basic account, with no administrator role and no permission on the server. The input comes from an attacker who calls the endpoints directly.

summary: A low-code platform for building language-model applications and agents has a node for connecting custom MCP servers, which can start a local process talking over standard input and output. The node checks the command against a short allowed list and blocks only a few environment variables, so a configuration that uses an allowed interpreter can set other environment variables, or exploit the process's root working directory, to make the interpreter run arbitrary system commands when the node refreshes its available actions. Preconditions: the local-process transport is enabled, which is the default; the attacker is an authenticated user able to edit a custom MCP node's configuration. The input comes from an attacker who reaches the configuration directly.

summary: A framework for agents that operate a computer's graphical interface asks a model for the next action and converts its response into executable code. It checks action syntax but does not bound parameters such as waiting time, scroll count or typed-text length. An attacker-supplied task prompt can cause the model to return an oversized action, tying up an execution worker and leaving subsequent tasks pending or timed out. Preconditions are access to a service accepting such task prompts, the low privileges listed by the record, and execution of the model-generated action in a worker serving other tasks. The attacker supplies the task text to the model; the model must generate the oversized action before execution produces the availability impact.

summary: A hosted coding agent runs in a cloud container with browser capability. Attacker-controlled web content loaded during an agent or browser flow can connect from inside that container to a local agent endpoint that requires no authentication. This permits code execution within the affected session and access to its files, repository contents, environment variables and credentials. Repository tokens provide access subject to their granted permissions; additional customer-configured secrets may extend the impact. Preconditions are a browser-capable configuration and a flow that loads attacker-controlled content. The record lists no privileges, passive user interaction and additional attack prerequisites. The triggering connection comes from the loaded web content; the advisory does not describe the model interpreting instructions to generate that connection.

summary: A visual platform for language-model agents has three MCP flaws. (1) On servers using the affected desktop operating system's command processor, an authenticated remote user supplies local-process server arguments using an alternate execution switch that the validator fails to recognize, allowing arbitrary commands. (2) An authenticated non-administrative user constructs a flow with an MCP tools component using a local subprocess transport. Execution bypasses two server restrictions and runs commands with the application's privileges, potentially exposing credentials and nearby services. (3) An unauthenticated attacker reaches publicly shared MCP project endpoints, where missing public-flow restrictions and session separation permit code execution and access to or modification of chat sessions. Each finding is triggered by attacker-supplied configuration or requests reaching the corresponding feature directly.

summary: A visual platform for language-model agents has five MCP flaws. (1) A network caller with low privileges can read server files through crafted resource-read requests, including uploaded documents, signing secrets, the database and environment variables. (2) The composer endpoint lacks valid sign-in checks when the composer is enabled, the default, and projects use OAuth; the source does not specify who supplies the triggering input. (4) Authenticated remote users can run commands through an insufficiently validated server-configuration command field. (5) Authenticated users can read, change or expose host files through container-based MCP servers whose volume and device arguments are insufficiently filtered. For findings one, three, four and five, attackers directly supply the requests or configuration.

summary: A self-hosted assistant that runs agents in containers can bridge to chat platforms; for some adapters it starts a temporary webhook on the loopback interface to receive forwarded button clicks. The webhook does not authenticate the sender and trusts the user identity written in the request body. A local process can therefore pose as the designated person and confirm a pending channel registration, wiring a channel to an agent group and adding the original sender to that group. Preconditions: a gateway-capable adapter that starts the webhook, a pending channel registration request, and the ability to run code on the same host and connect to the loopback address. The input comes from an attacker who reaches the webhook directly.

summary: A workflow automation platform exposes an MCP server with a tool that creates workflows from code. When a node's authentication type is written as an expression rather than a fixed value, the tool's credential check skips the test of which project owns a referenced credential. A credential from another project can then be saved as a reference on a workflow elsewhere; the execution path still blocks its use, so no secret is exposed. summary: A knowledge-base question-answering platform built on language models can publish applications that are also reachable as MCP servers. Application API keys set to expire are refused by the regular chat interface after expiry, but the MCP endpoint still accepts them. A holder of an expired key can keep listing the application's tool metadata and calling its tools, creating stored chat records. Preconditions: the attacker holds an application key that was once valid, the key is still marked active, it is non-permanent with an expiry in the past, and the target application is published; no administrator privilege is needed. The input comes from the key holder calling the endpoint directly.

summary: A command-line coding agent has two execution paths affected by repository content. (1) At session creation, it loads project-scoped MCP configuration and starts configured local server commands without first asking whether the workspace is trusted. An attacker-supplied repository configuration can therefore run commands with the developer's privileges when a session opens in the repository or a subdirectory, without a model call. The effect recurs on subsequent sessions. (2) The records also describe local utility lookup allowing an untrusted workspace to supply executables under common names before user confirmation. The executable must be selected during that lookup, but the sources do not specify the necessary search-path circumstances. The attacker supplies configuration for the first path and workspace executables for the second.

summary: An open platform for building and running general-purpose AI agents has a message queue interface that holds prompts waiting to be delivered to agent sessions. The interface checks sign-in but not ownership or account separation, so a logged-in user can list every user's pending prompts in one request, read or delete another session's queue, and add prompts to it. A background process then forwards added messages to the victim's running agent, which acts with the victim's credentials and permissions. Preconditions: an authenticated account on a shared multi-user deployment; for per-session reading, deleting or adding, the victim session's identifier; for the prompt-adding effect, a victim with a running agent. The input comes from an attacker who calls the interface directly.

An authenticated attacker can instead configure a malicious model server whose response bypasses the model entirely, or supply table-column names containing instructions the model reads. The record lists low privileges, conflicting with the unauthenticated route described in the advisory.
- For spreadsheet-file or online-table workflows containing loaded data, permitted library functions can send data out and request internal addresses, with further code execution described as possible. The attacker supplies a steering question to the reachable prediction endpoint, which requires no key by default; the model must generate and execute the resulting code.

summary:
A tool server that gives agents access to a service-discovery cluster connects to the cluster with an address and token from its own configuration. Two findings:
- Clients may override the backend address through a request header, and the destination is not restricted. A connected client can redirect the server's cluster traffic to its own endpoint, capturing the configured token, or make the server send requests to other reachable targets. This requires the server to be reachable by clients that are not fully trusted; token capture also requires a token configured in the server's environment.
- In stateless transport mode, per-client sessions are not isolated, so one client's authenticated cluster connection can be reused for another client's requests, and tool calls run with someone else's token. This requires stateless mode and more than one connecting client. The source does not say who supplies the input for this finding.

summary: A workflow automation library exposes its modules to agents through a generic tool that runs any module with model-chosen parameters, and also to clients of a hosted interface. summary:

summary: A client library for connecting agents to tool services caches identity tokens without separating them by intended audience.
